title: Identification of Compounds (Cations & Anions)
topic: Combined Tests for Unknown Ionic Compounds
subject: Combined Science (Chemistry)
constraints: No flame tests; limewater test described as 'white precipitate'

questions.question: A white solid is tested. When dilute HCl is added, effervescence occurs and the gas gives a white precipitate when bubbled through limewater. The solution obtained after adding HCl gives a white precipitate with NaOH that does not dissolve in excess. The solid is:
questions.explanation: Effervescence with HCl and white precipitate with limewater confirms CO₃²⁻. White precipitate with NaOH insoluble in excess indicates Ca²⁺. So compound is calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.

questions.question: A white solid is dissolved in water. The solution gives a white precipitate with acidified BaCl₂. Another portion gives a white precipitate with NaOH that dissolves in excess NaOH to give a colourless solution. The solid is:
questions.explanation: White precipitate with acidified BaCl₂ indicates SO₄²⁻. White precipitate with NaOH soluble in excess indicates Zn²⁺ (amphoteric hydroxide). Thus, the solid is ZnSO₄.

questions.question: A yellow-brown solution gives a reddish-brown precipitate with NaOH. Another portion gives a white precipitate with acidified BaCl₂. The compound is:
questions.explanation: Reddish-brown precipitate with NaOH indicates Fe³⁺. White precipitate with acidified BaCl₂ indicates SO₄²⁻. So the compound is iron(III) sulfate, Fe₂(SO₄)₃.

questions.question: A colourless solution gives a white precipitate with AgNO₃ that dissolves in dilute NH₃. Another portion gives a white precipitate with NaOH that dissolves in excess NaOH. The compound is:
questions.explanation: White precipitate with AgNO₃ soluble in dilute NH₃ indicates Cl⁻. White precipitate with NaOH soluble in excess indicates Zn²⁺ (amphoteric). So ZnCl₂ fits.

questions.question: A green solution gives a green precipitate with NaOH that turns brown on standing. Another portion gives a white precipitate with acidified BaCl₂. The compound is:
questions.explanation: Green precipitate (Fe(OH)₂) that turns brown (oxidised to Fe(OH)₃) indicates Fe²⁺. White precipitate with acidified BaCl₂ indicates SO₄²⁻. So FeSO₄.

questions.question: A white solid gives a pungent gas when warmed with NaOH. The gas turns moist red litmus paper blue. Its solution gives a white precipitate with AgNO₃ that dissolves in dilute NH₃. The solid is:
questions.explanation: Pungent gas turning moist red litmus blue indicates NH₃, confirming NH₄⁺. White precipitate with AgNO₃ soluble in dilute NH₃ indicates Cl⁻. So NH₄Cl.

questions.question: A blue solution gives a blue precipitate with NaOH that is insoluble in excess. Another portion gives a white precipitate with acidified BaCl₂. The compound is:
questions.explanation: Blue precipitate with NaOH indicates Cu²⁺. White precipitate with acidified BaCl₂ indicates SO₄²⁻. Thus, CuSO₄.

questions.question: A colourless solution gives a white precipitate with NaOH that dissolves in excess NaOH. The same solution gives a white precipitate with NH₃ that does not dissolve in excess NH₃. Another portion gives a white precipitate with acidified BaCl₂. The compound is:
questions.explanation: White precipitate with NaOH soluble in excess indicates Zn²⁺ or Al³⁺. White precipitate with NH₃ insoluble in excess distinguishes Al³⁺ (Zn(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NH₃). White precipitate with acidified BaCl₂ indicates SO₄²⁻. Thus, Al₂(SO₄)₃.

questions.question: A colourless solution gives a white precipitate with NaOH that does not dissolve in excess. The same solution gives no precipitate with NH₃. Another portion gives a white precipitate with AgNO₃ that dissolves in dilute NH₃. The compound is:
questions.explanation: White precipitate with NaOH insoluble in excess and no precipitate with NH₃ indicates Ca²⁺. White precipitate with AgNO₃ soluble in dilute NH₃ indicates Cl⁻. Thus, CaCl₂.

questions.question: A white solid is insoluble in water but dissolves in dilute HCl with effervescence. The gas produced gives a white precipitate when bubbled through limewater. When dilute H₂SO₄ is added to the resulting solution, a white precipitate forms. The solid is:
questions.explanation: Effervescence with HCl and white precipitate with limewater indicates CO₃²⁻. The resulting solution contains the cation. White precipitate with H₂SO₄ indicates Ba²⁺ (BaSO₄ is insoluble). CaSO₄ and ZnSO₄ are soluble. Thus, BaCO₃.
